main.text: [III, 271] Chapter II. [col. 454]
Some obscure passages of Scripture on Locusts are explained.

One may ask why, in the class of locusts or bruchi, the ילק jelek is called סמר samar, Jer 51:27, that is, φρίττων [phrittōn], bristling, or ὀρθόθριξ [orthothrix], horripilans [with hair standing on end], one whose hair stands erect with horror. So Job 4:15. When a spirit passed before me; תסמר שערת בשרי, the hairs of my flesh stood up. And Ps 119:120. סמר מפחדך בשרי, My flesh bristled for fear of thee. Here Symmachus has ὀρθοτριχεῖ [orthotrichei], and the Syriac ܣܦܣ [ספס]? — an elegant verb formed from the Hebrew noun קפוד, which means hedgehog. In the same way we say in French herisser, not from horrescere [to bristle], as some would have it, but from this very animal, which we call un herisson. The ancient Romans expressed it by a periphrasis, as the Poet:
I was stunned, and my hair stood on end. — —
And [col. 455]
And hair erect with horror. — —

But a later age said horripilare and horripilatio. Apuleius, in his third book, speaking of himself when changed into an ass: My ears bristle with immoderate growth. The old Glossaries: Horripilatur, ὀρθοτριχεῖ [orthotrichei]. The lexicon of Philoxenus: Ὀρθοτριχιῶ [orthotrichiō], horripilo. The Vulgate translator, Eccesiast. XXVII, 15.: Speech that swears much (I would read of one who swears much, as the Greek Λαλιὰ πολυόρκου [Lalia polyorkou]) will make the hair of the head stand on end, in Greek ὀρθώσει τρίχας [orthōsei trichas]. This condition does not seem applicable to a locust or a bruchus, since they are hairless. Therefore Castalio [=Sebastian Castellio, Latin Bible (1551)], Petrus Robertus, the English translators, and perhaps many others render it eruca [caterpillar], a very hairy little creature. Hence Columella in the Garden:
Nor do the slug wrapped in its shell and the hairy campedare to gnaw only the tender leaves.

Campe, that is, eruca, as he himself explains in his prose On the Cultivation of the Garden, near the end of book 12: Those which we call ERUCAE are named in Greek κάμπαι [kampai]. But one feature is not enough to establish this rendering when the others are lacking: for instance flight in the caterpillar, which is attributed to the jelek in Nahum III, 16. ילק פשט ויעף, Ielek spread itself out and flew away. Jerome elegantly, on chapter 4 of Amos: The caterpillar does not fly away like the locust, etc., but remains on the crops that are to perish, and with slow movement and sluggish bites consumes everything. Moreover, that Jeremiah compares the masses of horsemen rushing with great force upon the Babylonians to the bristling jelek [III, 272] does not seem to fit the caterpillar, which has nothing to resemble hostile bands.

Accordingly, for Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] and Tremellius [=Immanuel Tremellius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] ילק jelek is neither locust nor caterpillar, but melolontha, a little creature of which Hesychius says: Μηλολόνθη· εἶδος κανθάρων, οὓς τινες χρυσοκανθάρους λέγουσι [Mēlolonthē; eidos kantharōn, hous tines chrysokantharous legousi]. It is called melolontha, namely, because it is the bane of fruit; and chrysocantharus, as it were golden beetle, because it resembles a beetle in shape and gold in colour. Hence Aristophanes too, in the Wasps, calls it χρυσομηλολόνθιον [chrysomēlolonthion]. There the Scholiast: Ζωΰφιόν τί ἐστι κατὰ κάνθαρον ξανθὸν, ὃ καὶ κατέχοντες οἱ παῖδες δεσμοῦσιν ἐκ τοῦ ποδὸς, καὶ ἀφιᾶσι πρὸς τὸν ἀέρα [Zōyphion ti estin kata kantharon xanthon, ho kai katechontes hoi paides desmousin ek tou podos, kai aphiasi pros ton aera]; It is a little creature like a beetle, tawny, which boys catch, tie by the foot, and let go into the air. To this belong these lines of the same Aristophanes in the Clouds:
Ἀλλ᾽ ἀποχάλα τὴν φροντίδ᾽ ἐς τὸν ἀέρα, Λινόδετον ὥσπερ μηλολόνθην τοῦ ποδός· [All' apochala tēn phrontid' es ton aera, Linodeton hōsper mēlolonthēn tou podos;]

But let your care go into the air, like a cockchafer that has its foot tied with thread. There again the Scholiast says much the same as you read above. Julius Pollux and Suidas describe the same animal in much the same way. The former says that some write μηλολάνθην [mēlolanthēn] for μηλολόνθη [mēlolonthē] (rather μηλάνθην [mēlanthēn]), ἤτοι ἐκ τῆς ἀνθήσεως τῶν μήλων [ētoi ek tēs anthēseōs tōn mēlōn] (read μηλεῶν [mēleōn] with Eustathius) ἢ σὺν τῇ ἀνθήσει γιγνόμενον [ē syn tē anthēsei gignomenon], either from the blossoms of apple trees, on which Suidas reports that it settles, or because it is born together with the blossoms. If you take all this together, you will at once conclude that the little animal described is one far too well known to us Normans, to our very great harm: for every third year this pest grows worse on the blossoms of the apple trees, from which our most abundant produce comes ^{R1}. But I see no reason why ילק jelek should be thought to be the melolontha [cockchafer] rather than a kind of bruchus or locust. So all the ancients consistently render it, having been so taught by the Prophets themselves, who in many places of Scripture mention the jelek among the kinds of locusts. For examples see Ps 105:34. Joel 1:4 and II, 25. and Nahum III, 15. 16. One should therefore not lightly depart from this rendering. Indeed, even if it were granted (it is not conceded) that the jelek is the melolontha, the question posed, why the jelek is described as ὀρθόθριξ [orthothrix], would be solved no more easily. For the melolontha is no less smooth than the locust or the bruchus. Fuller [=Nicholas Fuller, Miscellanea theologica / sacra (1612–22)], it is true, who on this point sides with Junius and Tremellius in his Miscellanea, book 5, chapter 9, imagines that a cockchafer flying toward us, with the constant and rapid beating of its four wings, presents the appearance of a hedgehog [col. 456] bristling with spines standing out on every side.
[III, 273] Are we to believe it? Or do those who love invent dreams for themselves?

I, at any rate, do not see what soft wings, blunt at their tips, have in common with the spines of a hedgehog. And even if this were true, it would have been no reason for the recent translators to depart from the accepted rendering, since locusts and bruchi also have four wings, whose beating is as rapid as that of the cockchafer's wings. It would therefore have been just as easy to imagine the very same thing of locusts ^{R2}.

But to solve the question, there are two things we may answer. 1. It is not certainly established, as they would have it, that locusts of every kind are entirely smooth and hairless. At least I find in Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī] that قرن الجراد شعران في راسه [qarn al-jarād shaʿrān fī rāsih] is the name given to the horn of the locust, the two hairs which it has on its head ^{R3}: and on account of these, why should it not be said to bristle or to stand on end when it raises them upright? So Aelian writes of the haemorrhous in History, book 15, chapter 13: Φρίττει δὲ τὴν κεφαλὴν οἱονεὶ κέρασί τισιν [Phrittei de tēn kephalēn hoionei kerasi tisin]. Its head bristles as if with certain horns. Moreover, a poet of great name, Claudian, begins his description of the locust thus:
The crown of its head bristles, fierce eyes rise from the middle of its head, etc.

And in the Talmudic tractate Cholin, fol. 65, where some locusts are said to have גבחת gabbachath and others not to have it, there are those who understand a hump standing out on the back in the manner of a camel; among them is Baal Aruch [=the ʿArukh of Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome] [=Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome, the ʿArukh]. But for others גבחת is baldness, as the word is taken in other passages of the Talmud. Accordingly the marginal Gloss explains these Talmudic words about locusts, שאין לו גבחת, One that has no Gabbachath, thus: שאין ראשו מרוט, whose head is not bare. That is, in the Glossator's view, some locusts have a bare head, others a hairy one. Perhaps John alludes to this in Rev 9:8, when he attributes to those mystical locusts τρίχας ὡς τρίχας γυναικῶν [trichas hōs trichas gynaikōn], hair like the hair of women ^{R4}. Nor do I refer to anything else the fact that the Arabs [III, 274] call a kind of bruchus عرفان [ʿirfān] orphan, as if the name were formed from عرف [ʿurf] orph, that is, from a mane. Alcamus: العرفان جندب ضخم كالجرادة لا يكون الا في رمث او عنظوانة او دويبة صغيرة تكون برمل عالج او الدهنا [al-ʿirfān jundub ḍakhm ka-l-jarāda lā yakūnu illā fī rimth aw ʿunẓuwāna aw duwaybba ṣaghīra takūnu bi-raml ʿālij aw al-dahnā] Alorphan, a kind of bruchus as thick as a locust, usually found nowhere but in ramthsa and onduana (very sour plants, from eating which the belly of camels often swells). Or a small creature living in the sands of Aligi and Dahna: these are places near Medina. I add that in the same Alcamus الخنتف [al-khuntuf] alchanthapho is the name given to الجراد المنتف المنقي للطبخ [al-jarād al-muntaf al-munaqqā li-l-ṭabkh], a locust that is plucked and cleaned for cooking. This is the true explanation, since one who plucks his beard is also called الخنتوف [al-khuntūf] Alchanthouph. From this it plainly follows that some locusts are shaggy and hairy, which our interpreters had not known. Moreover, ילק סמר does not necessarily mean a locust ὀρθότριχα [orthotricha], since we bristle not only with our hair but with our whole body. For hair is not in question when David says, סמר מפחדך בשרי, My flesh bristled for fear of thee. So even a hairless locust can bristle: as when, struck with dread of an approaching enemy and fear of danger, it prepares [col. 457] to defend itself ^{R5}. And the Prophet, in the passage we are dealing with, could compare horsemen about to fall upon Babylon in great numbers with locusts and bruchi in such a state, against whose invasion it is difficult [III, 275] to defend oneself, as we shall show below. The passage reads: Appoint a commander against her. Bring up horses like bristling locusts: both in number and in their design of laying waste and destroying everything. What if the verbal noun סמר samar, which occurs nowhere else, means not so much bristling as horrifying, striking horror into anyone who sees it? This will fit a swarm of locusts exceedingly well, at whose onset ירגזון כל יושבי ארץ, all the inhabitants of the land tremble, Joel 2:1. Hence Hesychius, from some poet, as I suspect: Βρέττανα φοβερὰ [brettana phobera], a horrible locust.

Now we shall say what the ancients thought about this word, so that no one may tire himself in vain consulting them along with me. The Greeks, whom the Arab follows, have for כילק סמר ὡς ἀκρίδων πλῆθος [hōs akridōn plēthos], like a multitude of locusts, as if they had read ספר or מספר for סמר ^{R6}. Why the Chaldee has for ילק סמר זחלא דמצלהב, a gleaming or shining bruchus, no one could easily say. For gleam and shine have nothing in common with bristling and ὀρθοτριχίᾳ [orthotrichia]. Am I mistaken, or did he too read differently here, namely סגור for סמר, words very close in script? Now סגור is gold, Job 28:15 and throughout 1 Regum and 2 Paralipomenων. So ילק סגור would be a golden bruchus or golden locust, that is, of golden colour and shining like gold: such are the Arabian ones, of which Aelian, Historia book 10, ch. 13: Χρυσοειδῆ οὖν ἰνδάλματα καὶ ἐπ' αὐτῶν κατέστικται [Chrysoeidē oun indalmata kai ep' autōn katestiktai], They are marked with gold-coloured figures. And this very kind of locust could be called by the Chaldee מצלהב, shining, or, with one letter fewer, מצהב, gleaming with golden colour. If it is read so, this conjecture will be firmer. Jerome rendered like a spiny bruchus: with these words the holy man expressed neither the Hebrew adequately nor the nature of the thing. For bruchi or locusts are not distinguished by any stings, unless those mystical ones are meant, to which John attributes the stings of a scorpion, Rev 9:10^{R7}. The Syriac has only ܐܝܟ ܩܡܨܐ [איך קמצא], like a bruchus, omitting the following word סמר altogether, [III, 276] whether he did not read it or did not understand it. The Hebrews all render like a bruchus with bristling hair. But none of them explains why the bruchus is so called.

The locust is a wandering and unsteady animal, which is driven hither and thither at the slightest impulse and is carried anywhere with an easy leap or flight. Hence Iob. XXXIX, 20. (var. 23.) says of the horse, Have you made him move like a locust? that is, leap with equal agility. So in the Chaldee paraphrast on Jer 51:27. Let their horses come up מסככין הא כוחלא, leaping like locusts. Accordingly, just as in Hebrew חרגל chargol is a kind of locust, so in Arabic حرجل [ḥarjal] chargala is said of a horse that عدا يمينة أو يسرة [ʿadā yamīnatan aw yasratan], leaps to the right or to the left ^{R8}, a verb plainly made from the leap of the locust, as was noted in its place ^{a)}. And David says of himself, Psal. CIX, 23. I am shaken off like a locust, which, when it lacks a nest, wanders and is carried from hedge to hedge. For David is thought to have written this Psalm when, fleeing Saul, he ran about hither and thither without hearth and home. See Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra] and Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim]. So the Chaldee here has אטלטלת, I have wandered about. Quite foreign will seem the version of the Arabic of Savary, Like a locust, انتقضت [intaqaḍtu], I am consumed. But with one dot fewer it should be read انتفضت [intafaḍtu], I am shaken off, as in the Paris edition, and in the Syriac ܐܬܢܦܨܬ [אתנפצת], which is the same verb. In the Arabic MS. in my possession one reads قفزت [qafaztu], I leapt like a locust. This, though proper to the locust, does not suit this passage. [col. 458] But how wandering this animal is, how νομαδικὸν [nomadikon], and of uncertain abode, is nowhere taught so plainly as in Nahum ch. 3. There, after the Prophet has said to the city of Nineveh by way of concession (συγχωρητικῶς [synchōrētikōs]) in verses 15 and 16, Be as abundant as the bruchus, as numerous as the locusts, so that you multiply your merchants like the stars of heaven, he immediately adds by way of correction (κατ᾽ ἐπανόρθωσιν [kat᾽ epanorthōsin]), alluding to what he had said of the bruchus and the locusts: The bruchus, he says, has ravaged and flown away. Your princes shall be like locusts, and your captains כגוב גובי, like locusts; locusts, I say, which encamp in the hedges on a cold day; but when the sun rises they flee, and their place, where they were, is not known. As if he said: “You are indeed a most populous city, and your inhabitants seem to you equal in number to locusts. And within your walls many merchants and princes seek asylum, as locusts do in the hedges when they are cold. But there is no reason for you to trust in so numerous a multitude or in the wealth of these merchants, or to swell with pride at the strength of your princes and captains. For just as, when the sun rises, the locusts fly away and [III, 277] abandon the hedge that had been their refuge in the time of cold, so the peoples, merchants and princes who, when circumstances required, had fled to your walls, as soon as an occasion and hope of doing better elsewhere shines forth, will with one accord so abandon you that not even the least trace of them will remain.” Further, the Arabs elegantly express the flying away of locusts at sunrise by the verb اصقعر [iṣqaʿarra] ascaara. Alcamus: اصقعر الجراد اصابته الشمس وذهب [iṣqaʿarra al-jarād aṣābat-hu al-shams wa-dhahaba] Ascaara algirado, the sun struck the locusts and they went away. R. Selomo explains the words at the end of verse 15, התכבד כילק התכבדי כארבה, may you perish by sweeping away, as by the sweeping away of the bruchus and the locust. For these little creatures are wont to sweep everything away down to the dust, that is, to gnaw and scrape away everything in meadows, gardens and fields. Hence the Arabic name of the locust, جراد [jarād] girad, because the verb جرد [jarada] giarada, said of a field, means to make bare and to strip. But the verb התכבד in the sense of sweeping out occurs only among the Talmudists. Therefore others better refer it to abundance, which in Hebrew is כבד. And thus it coheres more fittingly with what follows, You have multiplied your merchants like the stars of heaven. What of the fact that in Exod 10:14 we read of the locusts, And the locust went up over all the land of Egypt, and settled in all the territory of the Egyptians, כבד מאד, very heavy, namely in its abundance? Thus it is evident that this very כבד pertains to the size of the multitude, and consequently so does the verb התכבד derived from it.

There are four animals whose wisdom Solomon, himself the wisest of kings, admires. Among them the locust has no king, ויצא חוצץ כלו, yet it goes out to war, each one dividing for itself, Prov 30:27, that is, the booty and the spoils of war, which is otherwise the prerogative of kings and commanders. Thus in Exodus XV, 9 Pharaoh says, I will divide the spoils, etc. And Moses, Joshua and David divide the booty among their people. In Hebrew idiom, to go out by itself often means to go out to war. So Gen 10:11. Out of that land he (Nimrod) went forth into Assyria, namely to make war. 2 Sam 11:1. At the time when kings go forth: that is, at the time when they are accustomed to set out for wars, as Jerome rightly says. Zech 14:3 The Lord went forth, he fought against the nations. Isa 42:13 The Lord goes forth as a mighty soldier. Ps 60:10 (var. 12.) Thou didst not go forth, O God, with our armies. So the locust, although ἀβασίλευτος [abasileutos], as the Greek translators have it here, nevertheless goes out, namely to war, חוצץ כלו, each one dividing for itself. For locusts do not wait for a commander to assign each of them a share of the booty: [col. 459] whatever part of the field they fly into, they hold it as their own, and there is no quarrel among them over the division of the booty. Hence, on the words of Isaiah, ch. XXXIII, v. 4, And your spoil shall be gathered as the gathering of the bruchus, the ancient Hebrews cited by Kimchi say: אמר להם נביא לישראל אספו שללכם אמרו לו לבוז או לחלק אמר להם אוסף [III, 278] החסיל מה אסיפת החסיל זה כל אחד ואחד לעצמו אף שללכם כל אחד ואחד לעצמו, The prophet said to the Israelites, „Gather your spoil.“ They said to him: „To plunder, or to divide?“ And he answered, „As the gathering of the bruchus.“ And what is the gathering of the bruchus? Each of them plunders for himself. So let each one of you seize his spoil for himself ^{R9}. We render the verb חצץ to divide, because it is the same as חצה, to halve and to divide; whence חצי, half. So Job XXI, 21. The number of his months (that is, his many months) חצצו, are cut in half. There חצצו stands for חצו. A parallel passage is Ps 55:24. Bloody and deceitful men לא יחצו ימיהם, shall not live out half their days. Therefore, since חצה refers to the division of booty when Moses is told in Num 31:27 וחצית את המלקוח, And thou shalt divide the booty, we think that τὸ [to] חוצץ here belongs to the same sense; all the more since among the Talmudists this very verb חוצץ is used of an arbiter who divides a disputed thing between the contending parties. As in Bava Bathra ch. 8.

[III, 279] fol. 133b חוצצין מחיצה לזה ומחיצה לזה, They divide half to this one, and half to that one. Such arbiters are called in the Gemara דייני דחצצתא, judges of division, or of halving. In Arabic too, حصّة [ḥiṣṣa], plural حصص [ḥiṣaṣ], is a portion of a thing; and the verb حصّ [ḥaṣṣa] in the third and sixth conjugations means to share and divide with another, in the fourth to give a portion to another ^{R10}.

[III, 280] Others interpret the passage of Solomon quite differently. The Greeks: Ἀβασίλευτόν ἐστιν ἡ ἀκρὶς, καὶ ἐκστρατεύει ἀφ᾽ ἑνὸς κελεύσματος εὐτάκτως [Abasileuton estin hē akris, kai ekstrateuei aph᾽ henos keleusmatos eutaktōs]. The Chaldee: The locusts, which have no king, are all gathered together at once, מתכנשין כלהון כחדא. So also the Syriac. And Jerome: The whole goes forth by its bands. And the Arabic: بعسكره امره واخذه بحسن ترتيب [bi-ʿaskarihi amruhu wa-akhdhuhu bi-ḥusn tartīb] In its camp is its affair, and its manner is with fine arrangement. To reconcile these ancient versions either with one another or with the Hebrew text would be very difficult. Yet Aben Ezra, coming close to the Chaldee, renders the Hebrew words ויצא חוצץ as יצא מאוסף ומקובץ, It goes out collected and gathered together. He tries to prove that חצץ is taken in this sense from the words of Job חדשיו חוצצו, that is, he says, נקבעו ונאספו, His months are gathered and collected. But we have shown that that passage must be rendered otherwise. And we deny that the Hebrew חצץ is used anywhere in this way. For Kimchi, in this passage חצץ means to divide herbs and the leaves of trees by cutting them off, so that the sense is: "The locusts have no king, yet they all go out to divide, that is, to cut off, leaves and herbs." In this version there are two things I find wanting. 1. These statements are ἀνακόλουθα [anakoloutha]. For why should locusts not feed and crop the grass even without a king? 2. חצץ does indeed mean to divide, as we have said, but not to cut off. Therefore a certain exceedingly learned man ^{R11}, who was not pleased with these interpretations, devised another: namely, that חוצץ is derived from the noun חץ, that is, arrow, as in Iud. III, 11. מחצצים, archers; and he explains the passage thus: The locusts have no king, yet they all go forth shooting arrows: that is (he says), darting themselves like arrows. But the Hebrew verb does not mean to shoot arrows; nor is it true, as he supposes, that to shoot arrows is the same as to dart oneself like arrows. Moreover, the flight of locusts is too slow to be compared with an arrow once shot. Finally, these do not [col. 460] cohere well enough: The locusts have no king, yet they all dart themselves like arrows. For birds do not need a king in order to fly swiftly. But he again supposes something further, namely that to dart oneself is the same as to wage war: which I would grant him far less than the earlier points.

If against Solomon's saying that locusts have no king one sets that statement of the Arabs about locusts in Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān], وهو من الحيوان الذي ينقاد لرئيسه فيجتمع كالعسكر اذا ظعن اوله تتابع جميعه [wa-huwa min al-ḥayawān alladhī yanqādu li-raʾīsihi fa-yajtamiʿu ka-l-ʿaskar idhā ẓaʿana awwaluhu tatābaʿa jamīʿuhu] [III, 281] جميعة ظاعنا واذا نزل اوله نزل جميعـه [jamīʿuhu ẓāʿinan wa-idhā nazala awwaluhu nazala jamīʿuhu] It is an animal of the kind that follows a leader and gathers like an army. For when the first of them departs, all follow and likewise depart. And when the first lodges, all the rest lodge too: I answer that the first locust, which the rest follow, is not regarded as a king, such as among bees is اليعسوب [al-yaʿsūb] ὁ ἐσσήν [ho essēn]. For among locusts the one that leads has not been chosen by tacit consent; rather, any one at all, as chance has it, departs or lodges first. To lodge in Arabic is نزل [nazala], that is, to descend onto a field so as to settle there for a time and be refreshed by feeding, as in an inn. In Greek you would say καταλύειν [katalyein]. Hence the son of Sirach says of snow, Ecclesiast. XLIII, 17. (var. 19.), Ὡς ἀκρὶς καταλύουσα ἡ κατάβασις αὐτῆς [Hōs akris katalyousa hē katabasis autēs]· Its descent is like a locust that lodges ^{R12}.

notes.text: It is easily understood that the melolontha is that green beetle, shining with a golden colour, which we call Goldkaefer, in LINNAEUS (Syst. Nat. T. I. vol. IV. p. 1580.) Scarabaeus scutellatus auratus.
notes.label: R1

notes.text: Oedmann [=Samuel Ödmann, Vermischte Sammlungen aus der Naturkunde] raised still more and weightier objections to the melolontha, Vermischte Sammlungen, Fasc. 2, p. 130 ff.
notes.label: R2

notes.text: EICHHORN, in his Commentar. in Apocalyps. T. II. p. 26, holds that the hair attributed to the locusts comes from the poet's own invention, because soldiers, to whom that whole comparison in John refers, were once adorned with long flowing hair, as Jerome attests on Ezechiel. XLIV, 20: to let the hair hang down — is properly the mark of the luxurious, of barbarians and of soldiers. But since not only Jeremiah (Chapter LI, vs. 27.) calls the locusts סמר, bristling, but Arab writers too attribute hairs to locusts, I think John alluded either to the antennae of real locusts, which, as we have just seen, the Arabs call two hairs, شعران [shaʿrān], or to the hairy head of certain species. Oedmann's conjecture, Fasc. 2, Chapter 6, pp. 147–149, that the Gryllus thorace spinis erectis coronatus of Linn. (Syst. Nat. T. I. vol. [III, 274] IV. p. 2066. ed. 13), whose antennae are three times longer than the body, was before the prophet's mind in this whole comparison, is very uncertain.
notes.label: R4

notes.text: "I would not wish this to have been written by a great man, for the comparison would thus be too feeble; it will not be vigorous enough even if, with others, you render horrible locust, toward which Bochart too finally inclines. For what Calvin notes, that the horses are here compared with locusts on account of their multitude, not their warlike strength, will, I believe, convince few. סוס, horse, must certainly be taken for cavalry. This is compared with ילק סמר, bristling locusts, stretching out their erect hairs, both for its multitude and dense columns, and for its warlike strength, laying waste everything, and for the darts and spears with which those forces bristled, according to that line of Virgil, Aeneid 10, 178: He leads a thousand in close array, with bristling spears. Here could also belong the gloss in the Qamus under the root سمر [smr], whose second conjugation is explained by Golius [=Jacobus Golius, Lexicon Arabico-Latinum (1653)], among other things, as he swiftly brandished an arrow. The more usual notion is he fastened or fixed with nails. That nail, specifically an iron one, is called مسمار [mismār], a meaning known also to the Hebrews, in the double form מסמר and מסמר 1 Chron. XXII, 3. Jer 10:4. Eccl 12:11. The participle is ܡܣܡܪܐ [מסמרא] מסמור, fixed with nails and, as it were, bristling. — — It is therefore quite probable that the verb סמר took on the sense of bristling from a nail sticking up, erect, projecting, so that it came to be said proverbially, סמר שערו, his hair resembled a fixed nail, was nailed. This becomes more probable from the use of שער זר for bristling hair. Cf. Genes. XXV, 28." Thus Schultens [=Albert Schultens, Liber Jobi (1737)] in his Commentar. [III, 275] ad Iob. 4, 15, p. 105. Jeremiah seems in this comparison to have had in view both the long and bristly antennae, which Arab writers call locks or hairs, and the hairy legs of certain species of locusts.
notes.label: R5

notes.text: But I. D. Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer], in his Observatt. Philologg. et Criticc. in Ierem. p. 393, rightly observes that this conjecture of Bochart's is hardly probable, since מספר signifies fewness. He himself thinks those translators understood a horrible locust, i.e. a horrible and countless swarm of them, from סמר, he bristled.
notes.label: R6

notes.text: That the Vulgate translator was thinking of the locusta aculeata, which ROESEL presents under the name locusta indica in Plate 6, Figs. 2 and 3, and §§ 41 and 42 of the preface to his Collection of locusts, is a hardly probable conjecture of I. D. Michaelis in the Supplemm. vol. IV. p. 1080, and in the Observatt. in Ierem. loc. cit.
notes.label: R7

notes.text: Schultens will give the whole passage of Firuzabadi in his Commentar. in Iob. p. 1130.
notes.label: R8

notes.text: The Hebrew words of Isaiah, ואסף שללכם אסף החסיל, your spoil shall be gathered with the gathering of the locust, can be referred to the locusts in either an active or a passive sense. In the former sense it will be a gathering of the locusts if these animals scrape off whatever they meet and strip it for their own use; in the latter it is the gathering of the locusts themselves, as they consume the crops, which is done by the farmers, who collect them in vessels or push them in heaps into ditches and pits to kill them. Forerius, a Spaniard by birth, observes on the passage of Isaiah that this is done in Africa and Spain. Cf. Io. Leonh. Frisch, Beschreibung von allerley Insecten (Berlin 1750), vol. 9, p. 9, and Gleditsch, Abhandlung von Vertilgung der Zugkeuschrecken, Berlin 1752, p. 59. Jerome took the same view, rendering the whole sentence thus: and your spoils shall be gathered together, as the bruchus is collected, as when the ditches have been filled with it. Ludov. Cappellus set out this sense more explicitly: this expression, he says, is taken from country people, who collect in heaps the bruchi and locusts that harm the crops, and trample them underfoot once collected. So the prophet means this: the Jews will easily and with no trouble, with no one hindering them, plunder your spoils from the camp, gather them together, and carry them off with them. Doederlein followed the same sense in his version of this passage, and Paulus [=H. E. G. Paulus, Clavis über die Psalmen (1791) and Clavis über den Jesaias (1793)] in his Clavis. But this interpretation is flatly contradicted by the second member, in which the locusts are introduced as being in action and motion, כמשק גבים שקק בו, running to and fro like the running to and fro of locusts, namely he runs to and fro, i.e. there is running to and fro in it. The sense of these words can scarcely be other than this: that the Israelites will gather the spoils of the fallen enemies, scattered over the fields, like locusts, and will run to and fro, leaping in the manner of those same locusts, as they gather them. Hence it is clear, from the law of the parallelism of members, that the gathering of the locusts in the first member is a gathering done by the locusts. Grotius also saw this, writing on this passage: „your spoils shall be gathered together, as the bruchus gathers, they will be gathered from you, the Assyrians, with as much impunity as the bruchus grazes on the plants. What follows in the Hebrew demands this interpretation.“ The prophet elegantly used the verb אסף, which is properly used of the gathering of crops and produce that takes place at harvest time. This the locusts do when in great swarms they settle on the fields and consume them.
notes.label: R9

notes.text: Alb. Schultens sought to confirm the same interpretation in his Animadverss. Philologg. in Iobum (which first appeared in 1709 and were reprinted in his Opera minora, Leiden 1769, p. 91. 92.) on ch. XL, 25, and on Proverb. XXX, 27, p. 258 f. of the Operr. minorr., and also in the Commentar. ad Proverb. p. 485, where he expresses the sense of this passage thus: the locust has no king, and yet this whole body divides the booty among themselves in equal portions, however dense and numerous it may be (for which reason it is called ארבה), so that this military and plundering throng seems to be held together as if under the strictest military discipline. But against this interpretation Schnurrer [=C. F. Schnurrer, Dissertationes philologico-criticae (1790)] rightly objects, in my judgement, in his Animadverss. ad quaedam loca Proverbiorum Salomonis, contained in his collected Dissertations, p. 108 f., not only that it is rather inapt to say that the locusts go out allotting booty, since booty is not divided immediately upon going out, but also that it is evident that something is praised in the locusts as worthy of admiration which otherwise, in any multitude, could be brought about and maintained only through the supreme authority of a commander to whom all are subject. Now the division of booty is not of the class of things that can in no way be accomplished without a commander. If indeed the distribution of booty among many is to be equal and just, then it is certainly necessary that someone be present who can govern the whole affair by his authority and keep each and every one to his duty. But of this equality of distribution there is nothing in the context of the passage. Schnurrer himself, after refuting the interpretation of Hunt, who, drawing on the Arabic حضّ [ḥaḍḍa], to incite, renders our words: they go out into battle line, at the war-signal of their whole army, proposes this sense: The locusts indeed have no king, yet they all go out in haste, taking here that meaning of the Arabic verb חצץ which consists in hastening. For this could be mentioned of the locusts as something singular and worthy of admiration: that the column of an immense multitude, although subject to no one by whose command and authority it is ruled, nevertheless of its own accord so unites and holds together that, when it must advance into battle, absolutely all, with none resisting or delaying, show themselves most prompt and most ready. This interpretation of Schnurrer, however, though approved by Döderlein and Dathe, displeased Ziegler in his Notis ad vers. teuton. Proverb. p. 365, because haste would bring in the notion of disturbance and confusion, which ought to be entirely foreign to this image. Yet what Ziegler himself puts forward, that the words חצץ כלו are to be rendered either in heaps and in crowds or each in its own place, does not commend itself to me more; for I can hardly see how this sense can be drawn from the meanings of the verb حصّ [ḥaṣṣa] that he himself cites, 1) he divided, 2) he obtained by lot. I interpret the words חצץ כלו: its whole body dividing itself, namely into bands, which Jerome also expressed: it goes out [III, 280] entire by its bands; on which words Grotius aptly remarks: „It is an animal ἀγελαῖον [agelaion] (gregarious), but ἀβασίλευτον [abasileuton] (without a king), as we had of the ant above, VI, 7. Locusts go in a great cohort, says Pliny.“
notes.label: R10

notes.text: Ludovicus de Dieu in Critica sacra on this passage.
notes.label: R11

notes.text: For locusts drop down after sunset, since the cold deprives them of the power of flight, as Le Brun, an eyewitness (αὐτόπτης [autoptēs]), observes in Voyages au Levante, p. 252. To this Nahum III, 17 alludes: Your nobles are like locusts, and your princes like a great swarm of locusts, which, when it is cold, cling to the hedges; when the sun rises they fly away, so that it is not seen where they were. In this passage the opposite expression שמש זרחה, the sun rises, shows that יום קרה, the time of cold, is not the cold days at the beginning of spring, as Harmar contends in his Observatt. super Oriente vol. I, p. 203 ff., but the evening time, after sunset. On these words Jerome says: For this is the nature of locusts, that, torpid in the cold, they fly about in the heat.
notes.label: R12
